title: The case, aloud
objectives: Work the whole case aloud and answer the interviewer's follow-ups with numbers.

screens.title: Fifteen minutes
screens.prose: This lesson takes about fifteen minutes; the case it rehearses runs fifteen more. The interviewer repeats: "Our boosted trees predict next-day returns. A researcher wants a network. You have fifteen minutes." The order of the conversation is `research-int` l11 to l15.
screens.question: What do you say in the first minute?

options.text: The target, horizon and loss, and that we decide by a paired test against the trees.
That networks are the modern choice and I would try one.
options.why: That is a preference before any evidence; frame the comparison first.

options.text: The network's architecture: layers, widths and dropout.
options.why: Architecture is the candidate's detail; the frame and the test come first.

hints.text: What must be agreed before anything is fitted?
What we predict and how we score it.
Frame, then say how the decision will be made.

feedback.correct: Frame first, with the decision rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Agree what "better" means first.

byKey.net: A preference is not a frame.

explain.text: The first minute sets the rules every later number is judged by. Each later step adds one number: a baseline score, a $t$, an interval.

screens.title: All four runs
screens.prose: Your evidence: two worlds, two seeds each, three models. Slide through the runs.
screens.question: In how many of the four runs is the paired $|t|$ above 2?

feedback.correct: 3 of 4: all but world B seed 1.

byKey.A: That counts only the two world A runs. World B seed 0 also has $|t| > 2$.

explain.text: Trees win world A clearly on both seeds; the network wins world B on seed 0 and leans its way on seed 1. That is the result to state, with its condition.

screens.title: Follow-up one
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: "What if the network wins only in one market regime, say high volatility?"
screens.question: Your answer?

options.text: Test that regime as a pre-stated split; if it holds, consider using the network only there.
Then switch entirely to the network, since it won in the regime you found.
options.why: A win in one regime says nothing about the others.

options.text: Ignore it: regimes are noise, and a win in one regime is not evidence.
options.why: Regimes can be real; test the split you name in advance, not one found afterwards.

hints.text: Was the regime chosen before or after looking?
A split found afterwards is a forking path.
Name it in advance and test it on fresh days.

feedback.correct: A pre-stated regime test, then a conditional model.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Treat the regime as a new hypothesis.

explain.text: A regime chosen after seeing results needs fresh data. If it holds, a regime switch between the two models is a legitimate design.

screens.title: Follow-up two
screens.prose: "How many seeds would you run?" Suppose per-seed $R^2$ gaps have mean 0.003 and sd 0.004. You want $t = \bar{g}/(s/\sqrt{k}) \ge 2$.
screens.question: What is the smallest number of seeds $k$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square $2s/\bar{g}$ and round up.

byKey.raw: Round up: 7 seeds give $t$ just under 2.
byKey.half: Square the ratio, do not halve it.

explain.text: $k \ge (2 \times 0.004/0.003)^2 = 7.11$, so 8 seeds; with so few, the $t$ bar is 2.36, not 2. Training seeds measure only the model's own randomness on one period, so whether a gap holds needs fresh periods, such as walk-forward folds or live shadow days. Say it as a formula, then the number: the interviewer wants the reasoning.

screens.title: Follow-up three
screens.prose: "Suppose the network wins on fresh data. What would you ship?"
screens.question: Order the rollout. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Run the network in shadow beside the trees, logging both forecasts.
Compare live daily errors and net P&L with the paired test.
Move a small share of capital to the network, with a stop rule.
Scale up while the live gap holds; keep the trees as the fallback.
Replace the trees in production on day one to save compute.
lines.why: A live switch with no shadow period risks the book on a backtest.

feedback.correct: Shadow, compare live, small capital, scale with a fallback.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Risk grows only as live evidence does.

byKey.rx: Day-one replacement skips the live test.

explain.text: A staged rollout turns the backtest into live evidence before money depends on it. The trees stay as a fallback.

screens.title: The model you prefer
screens.prose: A candidate opens with: "I would use a transformer; they are state of the art." Then looks for evidence.
screens.question: What is wrong with the order?

options.text: The conclusion came before the evidence, so every later number reads as advocacy.
Transformers are the wrong model family for return forecasting.
options.why: They may or may not help; the problem is answering before testing.

options.text: Nothing: confidence impresses interviewers, so naming the model first helps.
options.why: Confidence without a test reads as bias, which is what the case probes.

hints.text: What does the interviewer learn from that opening?
Frame and test first; conclude last.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at the order, not the model.

byKey.fine: The case tests method, not confidence.

explain.text: Opening with a model makes the rest look like a search for support. The structure itself shows judgement: frame, baseline, test, then the decision.

screens.title: A tie
screens.prose: Edge case: on fresh data the two models' daily errors differ by a mean of $0.0001$ with $t = 0.4$.
screens.question: What do you recommend?

options.text: Keep the trees: within noise, the simpler, proven model wins.
Switch to the network: it is not worse than the trees.
options.why: Switching has costs and risks; a tie gives no reason to pay them.

options.text: Average the two models' forecasts and use the blend instead.
options.why: Possible later, but it is a new model that needs its own test.

hints.text: With no difference, prefer what is already running and simpler.

feedback.generic: Not quite. What does a tie justify?

byKey.net: A tie is not a reason to pay the cost of switching.

explain.text: Within noise, the burden of proof is on the change. Keep the simpler model and say what evidence would reopen the question.

screens.title: Any "A or B"
screens.prose: The structure answers any model question: frame, baseline, incumbent, candidate, fair comparison, result with interval, decision with its condition, next step. $$\text{decision} = f(\text{paired evidence}, \text{costs}, \text{simplicity})$$
screens.question: Which question does this structure also answer?

options.text: "Should we replace our factor model with gradient boosting?"
"What is a factor model, and what does it assume?"
options.why: That is a definition question, not a comparison.

options.text: "Write a softmax that cannot overflow."
options.why: That is a coding task, l5's territory.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The structure is for choosing between two options.

explain.text: Replace "network" and "trees" with any candidate and incumbent: the eight steps and the paired test carry over unchanged.

screens.title: Credit spreads
screens.prose: A credit desk forecasts daily spread changes for 400 bonds with a linear factor model; a quant proposes gradient boosting. For more on interview loops like this, Chip Huyen's Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews is free online.
screens.question: Which baseline and test do you name first?

options.text: The linear factor model as incumbent, ridge as baseline, a paired test over days on a purged time split.
Boosting as the baseline, since it is the newer and more flexible of the two models.
options.why: The incumbent is the linear model; the new model must beat it.

options.text: A test over all bond-days pooled, which gives thousands of rows to test on.
options.why: Bonds on one day share market moves; test over days.

hints.text: Same structure: purged split, paired test over days.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Identify the incumbent and the unit of the test.

byKey.rows: Days are the independent unit here too.

explain.text: Only the names change: the incumbent is linear, the candidate is trees, and the paired test runs over days with a purge. With a multi-day horizon, the paired test would need a Newey-West standard error.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer closes: "Write it up for the head of research by tomorrow."
screens.question: What leads the note?

options.text: The recommendation and its condition, then the evidence from both worlds with intervals.
A full description of the network's architecture.
options.why: The reader decides on the result; method goes after, briefly.

options.text: Every number from every run, in a table, with no recommendation.
options.why: A note to a decision-maker leads with the decision.

hints.text: Who reads it, and what do they decide?
The head of research decides whether to switch.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Lead with what the reader must decide.

explain.text: The homework asks for exactly this note. Lead with the recommendation, give the evidence with intervals, and end with what would change your mind.

ideas: Say the case in order with a number at each step: frame, baseline, incumbent, candidate, comparison, result, decision, next step.
Our evidence: trees win world A ($t = 5.26$, $5.53$); the network leads world B ($t = -3.45$, $-1.91$).
A tie keeps the simpler incumbent; a win ships in stages with a fallback.

formula.name: Seeds needed
formula.note: For per-seed gaps of mean $\bar{g}$ and sd $s$, to reach $t \ge 2$. With few seeds the $t$ bar is above 2.

summary.trap: Naming the model you prefer before the evidence makes every later number look like advocacy.

quiz.question: In the case, which comes straight after naming the candidate model?

options.text: How the comparison will be run: split, purge, budget, seeds.
The decision on which model to ship, stated as the answer.
options.why: The decision needs the result first.

options.text: The next step: a shadow run, with a fallback if the model fails.

feedback.generic: Not quite. What do you need before any result?

explain.text: After the candidate comes the design of the comparison; only then a result, a decision and a next step.

quiz.question: Per-seed gaps have mean 0.002 and sd 0.003. How many seeds make $t \ge 2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square $2s/\bar{g}$ and round up.

quiz.question: Fresh data gives $t = -0.7$ for network minus trees. What do you recommend?

options.text: Keep the trees and gather more evidence if the question matters.
Switch: the network's difference is negative, so it is ahead.
Drop both models, since neither has beaten the other.
options.why: A tie between two models says nothing against both.

explain.text: A $t$ of $-0.7$ leans to the network but is well within noise, so the burden of proof stays with the change.
